figures.name: Anzû
figures.title: The Storm Bird
figures.domain: Storms, wind, theft of the Tablet of Destinies
figures.figureDescription: A mythical bird-demon of the ancient Near East, Anzû is a colossal storm bird with the head and wings of an eagle and the body of a lion. In the Babylonian epic, he steals the Tablet of Destinies from the god Enlil, plunging the universe into chaos until the warrior god Ninurta slays him.

figures.name: Lamashtu
figures.title: The Child-Devouring Demoness
figures.domain: Disease, death of infants, poisoning of rivers
figures.figureDescription: A fearsome demoness who preyed upon pregnant women and newborn children. Daughter of the sky god Anu, she was depicted with a lioness head, donkey teeth and ears, hairy body, and long fingers with sharp nails. She was propitiated by amulets bearing the image of her foe Pazuzu.

figures.name: Lamassu
figures.title: The Protective Spirit
figures.figureDescription: A celestial protective spirit depicted as a winged bull or lion with a human head, Lamassu statues flanked the entrances of Assyrian palaces and cities to ward off evil. Despite their demonic appearance in modern terms, they were benevolent guardians in Mesopotamian belief.

figures.name: Pazuzu
figures.title: King of the Demons of the Wind
figures.figureDescription: King of the demons of the southwest wind, Pazuzu was both feared and invoked for protection. He had a canine face, bulging eyes, a scaly body, lion's paws, eagle talons, and a scorpion's tail. Despite being a bringer of plague, amulets of Pazuzu were used to ward off his rival Lamashtu.

figures.name: Qingu
figures.title: Champion of Tiamat
figures.figureDescription: A demon or god of chaos who served as Tiamat's champion in the Babylonian creation epic Enuma Elish. After Tiamat forged eleven monsters to wage war against the younger gods, she appointed Qingu as their supreme commander. When Marduk slew Tiamat, he took the Tablet of Destinies from Qingu and defeated him.

figures.name: Hanbi
figures.title: Father of Pazuzu
figures.figureDescription: An evil demon lord, Hanbi is known primarily as the father of Pazuzu. In incantation texts, he is invoked alongside his son as a powerful malevolent force, though his independent mythology is sparse.

figures.name: Kūbu
figures.title: Ghost of the Stillborn
figures.figureDescription: The spirits of children who died before or shortly after birth in ancient Mesopotamian belief. Kūbu were thought to dwell in the netherworld and could cause misfortune if not properly propitiated through ritual.

figures.name: Kilili
figures.title: The Owl Demoness
figures.figureDescription: A demoness associated with owls and the night, Kilili was considered an harbinger of ill fortune. She appears in akītu festival incantations as one of the demonic forces driven out during the New Year purification rites.

figures.name: Dimmeku
figures.title: Underworld Demoness
figures.figureDescription: An underworld demoness invoked in healing incantations. Dimmeku was associated with the dark forces that caused illness and madness, and was counteracted through ritual binding and exorcism.

figures.name: Latarak
figures.title: The Lion Protector
figures.figureDescription: A lion-bodied protective deity or monster invoked in apotropaic rituals. Latarak was believed to ward off evil spirits and was depicted in boundary stones and protective figurines.

figures.name: Sebitti
figures.title: The Seven Warrior Demons
figures.figureDescription: A group of seven demonic warrior gods, sons of the god Erra. The Sebitti were fearsome agents of destruction who accompanied Erra in his destructive rampage across Mesopotamia, as recounted in the Erra Epic. Each bore a different weapon and aspect of devastation.

figures.name: The Four Winds
figures.title: Wind Demons
figures.figureDescription: In Mesopotamian cosmology, the four cardinal winds were sometimes personified as demonic forces. They were unleashed during divine punishment and cosmic upheaval, and had to be controlled or bound by the gods to maintain order.

figures.name: Šeri and Ḫurri
figures.title: Bull Servants of the Storm God
figures.domain: Storm service, cattle of the gods
figures.figureDescription: A pair of bull demons who served as the cattle herds of the storm god. Šeri (Day) and Ḫurri (Night) represented the alternation of day and night and the restless energy of the storm.

figures.name: Ugur
figures.title: Divine Weapon
figures.figureDescription: A divine weapon-deity personified as a snake-dragon, Ugur served as the weapon of the god Nergal in the underworld. In the Erra Epic, Ugur is one of the weapons unleashed during the god Erra's destructive war.

figures.name: Sisig
figures.title: Apotropaic Spirit
figures.figureDescription: An apotropaic spirit invoked in protective rituals and incantations. Sisig was called upon to turn back evil and was part of the complex Mesopotamian system of supernatural defense against malevolent forces.
